title: Does Alcohol Help a Headache? Why Wine or Beer Usually Backfires
excerpt: Can a glass of wine or a beer help a headache? Why alcohol can feel like it helps, why it usually makes headaches worse, what not to mix it with, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can wine or beer help a headache? Why alcohol may numb pain briefly but usually makes it worse, which painkillers not to mix, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer is no.** Alcohol doesn't treat a headache, and for a lot of people it makes one worse. A drink can feel like it helps for a little while, because alcohol has a mild numbing effect at higher doses and it relaxes you. But alcohol also widens blood vessels, dehydrates you, wrecks your sleep, and is one of the best-known headache triggers there is. The relief, if you get any, tends to be short. The rebound tends to be longer.

That's true whether the drink is wine, beer, or spirits. Red wine in particular is one of the drinks people most often name as a headache trigger, so reaching for a glass to fix a headache is a bit like using a match to put out a fire.

This guide explains why a drink can *feel* like it helps, why it usually backfires, what to do if you have a headache and you're out for the evening, which painkillers you shouldn't mix with alcohol, and the warning signs that mean a headache needs a doctor.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information for social drinkers, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** for a sudden, severe headache that reaches full strength within about a minute (often described as "the worst headache of my life"), a headache after a fall or any blow to the head, or a headache with fever and a stiff neck, confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, vision loss, a seizure, or fainting. These are not hangover symptoms. Falls are common when people have been drinking, so don't write off a headache after a bump to the head. **See a doctor soon** if your headaches are new, getting more frequent or severe, waking you up at night, or showing up after even small amounts of alcohol. And if you get headaches along with shaking, sweating, racing heart, or anxiety when you stop drinking after a stretch of daily drinking, that can be alcohol withdrawal. Talk to a doctor rather than stopping suddenly on your own, because withdrawal can become dangerous.

## Does Alcohol Help a Headache? What Actually Happens in Your Body

To understand why a drink is a poor headache remedy, it helps to know what alcohol does once it's in your bloodstream.

**It widens blood vessels.** Alcohol is a vasodilator, meaning it relaxes the walls of blood vessels and lets them open up. That's why your face can flush and feel warm after a drink. In the head, widening of blood vessels and the chemical signals that go along with it can set off the brain's pain pathways, especially in people prone to migraine. Researchers no longer think migraine is *only* about blood vessels, but vessel changes and the nerve signals around them are part of the picture.

**It dehydrates you.** Alcohol lowers a hormone called vasopressin, whose job is to tell your kidneys to hold onto water. With less of it, you make more urine and lose fluid faster than you're taking it in. Dehydration on its own can cause a headache, and it can make an existing one worse. (We go into more detail in our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).)

**It disrupts sleep.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it fragments sleep in the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. Poor sleep is a common headache trigger, and many people with migraine know that a short or broken night can bring one on.

**It leaves behind by-products.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that's linked to flushing, nausea, and headache. Many drinks also contain congeners, which are other substances made during fermentation and aging. Darker drinks such as red wine, whiskey, and brandy tend to have more of them than clear drinks such as vodka.

**It triggers specific headache disorders.** Alcohol is one of the most commonly reported migraine triggers. For people with cluster headaches, alcohol is a classic trigger during a cluster period, sometimes within an hour of a single drink.

None of this sounds like something that would cure a headache, and it isn't.

## Why a Drink Can *Feel* Like It Helps

People who say a drink helps their headache aren't imagining things. There are a few real reasons a drink can seem to take the edge off.

### Alcohol has a mild short-term numbing effect

Alcohol does have a pain-dulling effect. A 2017 meta-analysis of experimental studies in *The Journal of Pain* found that alcohol modestly raised people's pain threshold, with the effect showing up at blood alcohol levels around the legal driving limit in many countries. In other words, the numbing only arrives at the point where you're already impaired, and it fades as your blood alcohol falls. That's also when the dehydration, poor sleep, and by-products start to work against you.

So if you have a dull headache and you drink enough to feel tipsy, you may notice the pain less for a while. That isn't treatment. It's borrowing against later.

### It relaxes you

A lot of everyday headaches are tension-type headaches, the band-like ache across the forehead or the back of the head that comes with stress, long hours at a screen, or tight neck and shoulder muscles. Alcohol is a sedative, and that first drink at the end of a hard day can make you feel looser. If your headache is mostly stress, feeling calmer may make it feel smaller.

The trouble is that the same relief comes from things that don't backfire: stepping away, stretching your neck and shoulders, a walk, a shower, food, or simply sitting somewhere quiet. And if you get used to treating stress headaches with a drink, you can end up with more headaches, not fewer.

### You often drink fluid and eat at the same time

If you sit down with a glass of wine, there's a decent chance you're also eating dinner and drinking a little water, and you've stopped doing whatever you were doing before. Low blood sugar and mild dehydration are both common headache triggers. The food and fluid may be doing more of the work than the wine.

### You might be pushing back a hangover

If the headache is from drinking the night before, another drink really can make you feel better for a while. That's the "hair of the dog" effect, and we cover it in its own section below.

## Can Wine Help a Headache?

This is one of the most common versions of the question, and the answer is a clear no. There is no good evidence that wine relieves headaches, and red wine is one of the drinks most often reported as a headache trigger.

People who get headaches from red wine have offered plenty of explanations over the years. The ones you'll hear most:

- **Histamine.** Red wine contains more histamine than white wine. Some people break histamine down more slowly than others, and histamine can cause flushing and headache.
- **Tyramine and other amines.** These are naturally occurring compounds found in aged and fermented foods and drinks. Some people with migraine report sensitivity to them.
- **Tannins and other plant compounds.** Red wine is fermented with grape skins, which gives it more tannins and flavonoids. Some researchers have suggested certain flavonoids may interfere with how the body processes alcohol, letting acetaldehyde build up.
- **Sulfites.** Sulfites get blamed a lot, but they're probably not the main culprit for most people. White wine often contains as much sulfite as red, or more, and many dried fruits contain far more than wine does. A true sulfite sensitivity more often causes breathing problems such as wheezing in people with asthma.

The honest summary is that the exact cause of red wine headache is still debated, and it may be different for different people. What isn't really debated is that red wine is a poor choice if you already have a headache. If you want the full picture, see our guides on [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) and [whether sulfites in wine cause headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches).

### What about white wine or a "clean" wine?

White wine tends to have less histamine and fewer congeners than red, and some people who react to red wine do fine with white. But white wine is still alcohol, so it still widens blood vessels, dehydrates you, and disrupts sleep. Labels such as "clean" or "low-sulfite" are mostly marketing, and there is no good evidence that they make wine safe to drink with a headache.

## Does Beer Help a Headache?

No. Beer is lower in alcohol per serving than wine or spirits, so one beer contains less alcohol than a large glass of wine. But it is still alcohol, and it still has the same basic effects. Beer also contains a lot of fluid, which might sound like it should help with dehydration, but alcohol's effect on your kidneys means you tend to lose more fluid than the beer puts in.

Some people find certain beers more likely to give them a headache than others. Darker and stronger beers usually carry more congeners and more alcohol. We go into the details in our guide on [beer headaches](/never-hungover/beer-headache).

## What About Spirits? Is Whiskey or Vodka Any Different?

The dose of alcohol matters more than the type. A standard shot of spirits contains about the same amount of alcohol as a standard glass of wine or a regular beer. Clear spirits such as vodka and gin contain fewer congeners than dark spirits such as whiskey, bourbon, or brandy, and some studies have found that drinks high in congeners lead to worse hangovers at the same alcohol dose. But a vodka is still a vasodilator and a diuretic. Switching to clear spirits doesn't turn a drink into a headache remedy.

## The Two Kinds of Alcohol Headache

The International Headache Society, which publishes the standard classification doctors use for headache disorders, recognizes two kinds of headache caused by alcohol:

| Type | When it starts | What it's like |
|---|---|---|
| **Immediate alcohol-induced headache** (sometimes called a "cocktail headache") | Within about 3 hours of drinking | Often throbbing, on both sides of the head, and worse with movement. Less common, and more likely in people prone to migraine. |
| **Delayed alcohol-induced headache** (the hangover headache) | About 5 to 12 hours after drinking, usually the next morning as blood alcohol falls | Throbbing or pressing, often with fatigue, nausea, thirst, and sensitivity to light and noise. Usually clears within a day, and the classification says it should resolve within 72 hours. |

The immediate type matters for this question. If you're someone who gets a headache within a couple of hours of drinking, adding more alcohol to an existing headache is the opposite of what you want. If you've noticed you get a headache after just a small amount, our guide on [headaches after one drink](/never-hungover/headache-after-one-drink) covers what might be going on.

## Alcohol and Migraine: A Common Trigger

If you get migraines, drinking to relieve one is especially likely to backfire. Alcohol is among the triggers that people with migraine report most often, and red wine comes up more than any other drink. Not everyone with migraine reacts to alcohol, and the same person may react on some days and not others, often depending on other triggers stacking up at the same time: stress, poor sleep, skipped meals, or hormonal changes.

A few practical points for people with migraine:

- **Don't use alcohol as a migraine treatment.** If you have a prescribed migraine medicine, use that, and ask your doctor or pharmacist whether alcohol is okay with it.
- **Notice your own pattern.** A simple headache diary (what you drank, how much, what you ate, how you slept) can show whether a particular drink or amount sets you off.
- **Some people do better with less, not none.** If you get migraines after red wine but not after a small glass of something else, that's useful information. But there's no drink that's guaranteed safe for everyone.

Our guide to [migraines after drinking](/never-hungover/migraine-after-drinking) goes into this in more depth.

## Alcohol and Cluster Headaches

Cluster headaches are rare but extremely painful. They cause severe pain around one eye, often with a watering eye and a runny or blocked nostril on the same side, and they come in "clusters" of attacks over weeks or months. Alcohol is a well-known trigger during a cluster period, and many people with cluster headaches find that even a small drink can bring on an attack quickly. Outside a cluster period, the same drink often causes no problem. If you have, or think you might have, cluster headaches, alcohol during an active period is best avoided, and a doctor can help with proper treatment.

## Does Hair of the Dog Help a Hangover Headache?

"Hair of the dog" means having a drink the morning after to ease a hangover. It can feel like it works, and there's a reason for that. A hangover peaks as your blood alcohol falls back toward zero. When you drink again, your blood alcohol rises, and the withdrawal-like part of the hangover (the shakiness, irritability, and some of the headache) eases for a while.

But you haven't fixed anything. You've pressed pause. When the new alcohol wears off, you're back where you started, often more dehydrated and more tired. There is no good evidence that a morning drink treats a hangover, and making it a habit can become its own problem. If you find you *need* a drink in the morning to stop shakiness or feel normal, that's a sign worth talking to a doctor about.

For a closer look, see our guide on [whether hair of the dog works](/never-hungover/does-hair-of-the-dog-work).

## Don't Mix Alcohol With Headache Medicine

This is the most important practical point in the whole article. If you've taken something for a headache, don't then add alcohol, and if you've been drinking, be careful about what you take. Here's why, by type. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about your own situation, especially if you take other medicines or have a health condition.

**Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs).** These are easier on the liver than acetaminophen, but they're hard on the stomach lining. Their US labels carry a stomach-bleeding warning for people who have 3 or more alcoholic drinks a day. Alcohol already irritates the stomach, so the two together raise the risk of irritation and bleeding. NSAIDs can also strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated. More in our guides to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol).

**Acetaminophen (Tylenol, paracetamol).** Your liver processes both acetaminophen and alcohol, and regular heavy drinking makes the liver more vulnerable to acetaminophen damage. The US label warns people who have 3 or more drinks every day to ask a doctor before using it. One normal dose the morning after a few drinks is unlikely to harm a healthy adult who doesn't drink heavily, but never take it "just in case" before bed after drinking. See our full guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

**Combination headache pills (such as Excedrin).** Many contain both acetaminophen and aspirin, plus caffeine. That means you carry both sets of risks at once, and it's easy to double up on acetaminophen without realizing it. Our guide to [Excedrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/excedrin-and-alcohol) covers this.

**Prescription headache and migraine medicines.** Some prescription headache treatments, especially those that contain butalbital or opioids, are sedating, and combining them with alcohol can slow your breathing and cause dangerous drowsiness. Others, including some preventive migraine medicines, can make you more sensitive to alcohol. Check the label and ask your pharmacist.

**Nighttime cold and sleep products.** Products labeled "PM" or "night" often contain a sedating antihistamine, and many also contain acetaminophen. Alcohol is a sedative too, so stacking them can leave you more impaired than you expect.

The simplest rule: **pick one.** If you need a painkiller, skip the drink. If you've been drinking, wait until the alcohol has cleared and you've eaten before taking anything, and take a single standard dose.

## You Have a Headache and You're Going Out. What Now?

Sometimes the headache is already there and you've got plans. Here's a sensible way to handle it.

1. **Drink a big glass of water and eat something first.** A lot of afternoon and evening headaches come from mild dehydration and low blood sugar. Give those a chance to settle.
2. **If you need a painkiller, take it and then skip alcohol for the evening.** That's the safest combination. If that's not realistic, at least don't take the pill and then start drinking right away. Ask a pharmacist what's safe for you.
3. **If you do drink, go slow and small.** Choose a lower-alcohol drink, avoid the drinks that usually trigger you (red wine is a common one), alternate every drink with a glass of water, and stop early if the headache starts building.
4. **Watch the caffeine.** A coffee can help some headaches, but caffeine plus alcohol can leave you feeling more alert than you really are, which makes it easier to drink more than you meant to. Our guide to [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol) explains why.
5. **Go home if it's getting worse.** A headache that grows through the evening while you're drinking is your body telling you something.

## What Actually Helps a Headache (Without the Drink)

For the ordinary headache most people get, the basics work better than alcohol and don't come with a rebound.

- **Water and electrolytes.** If you might be dehydrated, drink water steadily. After drinking or sweating, an oral rehydration or electrolyte drink can help. See our [electrolyte drinks compared](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).
- **Food.** A proper meal, especially if you've skipped one.
- **A standard dose of an over-the-counter pain reliever**, taken without alcohol, following the label. Don't take them most days, because frequent painkiller use can itself lead to more frequent headaches (doctors call this medication overuse headache).
- **Rest in a dark, quiet room** for migraine-type headaches.
- **A cold pack on your forehead or the back of your neck**, or a warm one on tight neck and shoulder muscles.
- **Moderate caffeine**, such as a cup of coffee, if you usually drink it. Missing your normal coffee can cause a headache on its own.
- **Gentle movement and stretching** for tension-type headaches.
- **Sleep.** If you're short on it, it may be the real cause.

If you regularly wake up with a headache after drinking, the most effective change is the plain one: drink less, drink more slowly, eat before and during, and alternate with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, and our explainer on [why alcohol causes headaches](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) goes deeper into the causes. If the headache has already arrived, see our [hangover headache relief guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).

## Who Should Be Especially Careful With Alcohol and Headaches

Drinking with a headache is a worse idea than usual if you:

- **Get migraines or cluster headaches.** Alcohol is a common trigger for both.
- **Have already taken a painkiller or other medicine** in the last several hours.
- **Have a stomach ulcer, acid reflux, liver disease, or kidney disease.**
- **Take blood thinners, sedatives, sleep medicines, or certain antidepressants**, which can interact with alcohol.
- **Are pregnant or trying to become pregnant.**
- **Hit your head** earlier in the day or evening.
- **Have a headache that's different from your usual ones.** A new type of headache deserves attention, not a drink.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take before or while drinking. Research has focused on how it may affect alcohol metabolism and the brain's response to alcohol, but most of that evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM treats a headache, and it doesn't make it safe to mix alcohol with painkillers.

If you're a social drinker who wants to add it to a broader routine of eating, hydrating, and pacing yourself, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Treat it as an optional extra, not a fix.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol doesn't treat headaches. Any relief is short, and the rebound from dehydration, poor sleep, and widened blood vessels often makes the headache worse later.
- Wine, especially red wine, is one of the most commonly reported headache triggers. Beer and spirits aren't remedies either.
- Alcohol is a well-known trigger for migraine and cluster headaches.
- Hair of the dog only postpones a hangover headache.
- Don't combine alcohol with headache medicine. Pick one, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.
- Water, food, rest, and a standard dose of an over-the-counter pain reliever (without alcohol) work better.
- Get emergency care for a sudden, severe headache, a headache after a head injury, or a headache with fever, stiff neck, confusion, weakness, or vision changes.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol help a headache?**

Not in any reliable way. Alcohol has a mild, short-lived numbing effect at higher doses and can make you feel more relaxed, so a drink may seem to take the edge off for a while. But alcohol widens blood vessels, dehydrates you, disrupts sleep, and is a well-known trigger for migraine and cluster headaches. For many people it makes the headache worse later, and it adds risk if you've already taken a painkiller.

**Can wine help a headache?**

There is no good evidence that wine relieves headaches. Red wine in particular is one of the drinks people most often name as a headache and migraine trigger. A glass of wine may feel relaxing if your headache is stress-related, but water, food, rest, and a standard dose of an over-the-counter pain reliever (taken without alcohol) are far more dependable.

**Does beer help a headache?**

No. Beer contains less alcohol per serving than wine or spirits, but it still contains alcohol, which can widen blood vessels and trigger headaches in people who are prone to them. Beer also makes you urinate more, which can leave you dehydrated. Any brief relief usually comes from relaxation or the fluid, not from the beer itself.

**Is it okay to drink alcohol after taking ibuprofen or Tylenol for a headache?**

It's best to avoid it. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin carry label warnings about stomach bleeding for people who have 3 or more drinks a day, and alcohol already irritates the stomach. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and alcohol both put work on the liver, and the label warns people who have 3 or more drinks a day to ask a doctor first. If you've taken a painkiller, skip the drink. Ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Does hair of the dog help a hangover headache?**

Only in the sense that it postpones the hangover. As your blood alcohol rises again, you may feel briefly better, but the headache, dehydration, and poor sleep come back once that alcohol wears off, often worse. There is no good evidence that a morning drink treats a hangover, and making it a habit is a warning sign worth taking seriously.

**Why does alcohol give me a headache even after one drink?**

Some people are simply more sensitive. Alcohol widens blood vessels and can set off the brain's pain pathways in people prone to migraine or cluster headaches, and some drinks contain other compounds, such as histamine, tyramine, or congeners, that may add to the effect. The International Headache Society recognizes a headache that comes on within about three hours of drinking as its own type, separate from a hangover headache.

**When should I see a doctor about a headache and alcohol?**

Get emergency care for a sudden, severe headache that peaks within a minute, a headache after a fall or head injury, or a headache with fever and stiff neck, confusion, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, vision loss, or fainting. See a doctor soon if your headaches are new, getting more frequent, or keep happening after small amounts of alcohol. If you get headaches, shakes, sweating, or anxiety when you stop drinking after a period of daily drinking, talk to a doctor rather than stopping suddenly on your own.

**Can DHM stop an alcohol headache?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats alcohol-related headaches specifically. DHM (dihydromyricetin) has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. Some people take it before or while drinking as part of a broader routine, but it doesn't replace drinking less, staying hydrated, and eating.
